ideas.title: The AI Lab That's Funding Its Own Landlord
ideas.trend: Anthropic committed $200B to Google Cloud over five years this week, per The Information, while Google holds up to $40B in Anthropic equity — formalizing a circular investor-customer-competitor structure.
ideas.consensus: Anthropic is the safety-focused independent AI lab, OpenAI's most serious challenger, with its own capital base and values.
ideas.angle: The biggest independent AI labs aren't independent. They're feudal arrangements where hyperscalers own both the infrastructure and the equity. The independence is the pitch deck. The structure is a loop.

content_pack.x_longform:
The AI lab that positions itself as Google's most dangerous competitor just committed to spending $200 billion on Google's infrastructure.

Per The Information this week, Anthropic agreed to a five-year, $200 billion cloud deal covering compute access, Broadcom-built TPU chips, and data center capacity coming online from 2027. Google holds up to $40 billion in Anthropic equity, with further funding tied to performance milestones. Anthropic is now Google's largest contracted cloud customer. Also its most significant AI equity investment. Also its most credible frontier model competitor.

The $200 billion commitment represents more than 40 percent of the $460 billion in remaining performance obligations Google disclosed to investors last quarter. Contracts from Anthropic and OpenAI combined now account for more than half of the $2 trillion in cloud backlogs across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Platform.

Anthropic also runs a parallel arrangement with Amazon. More than $100 billion committed to AWS over a decade. Amazon holding a $25 billion stake in exchange.

Add the two infrastructure commitments together: roughly $40 billion per year to Google, $10 billion per year to Amazon, against Anthropic's annualized revenue of around $19 billion. The math closes only if Anthropic grows revenue three to four times and holds margins, or if the investors keep funding the gap. The investors funding the gap are the same companies collecting the cloud bills.

The dollar moves in a circle. Google invests in Anthropic. Anthropic scales on Google compute. Google's cloud revenue grows. Google's equity appreciates. The same capital loops.

Microsoft ran this architecture with OpenAI starting in 2023. Thirteen billion invested. Azure as exclusive cloud provider. Today OpenAI is Azure's largest workload, and Microsoft's stake has become one of its most valuable strategic assets. The framing at announcement was partnership. The structural reality: investor collects the infrastructure margin while the lab scales.

This week the Pentagon announced AI contracts with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Amazon, Oracle, SpaceX, and Reflection. Anthropic was excluded, after refusing to drop safety guardrails from AI used in warfare applications. The Pentagon exclusion caps one revenue category. The cloud dependency caps the full cost structure. Both at once.

The architecture matters for valuation. Anthropic sits at a $61 billion valuation on the premise that it captures the economic surplus from frontier AI. A structurally independent Anthropic could retain a large share of that surplus. An Anthropic whose full compute stack runs on infrastructure priced and owned by its investors captures whatever margin those investors allow. The ceiling is Google's decision.

The Softbank playbook from 2017 to 2022 showed how strategic investor relationships behave when conditions shift. Softbank funded startups and connected them to portfolio companies as customers. Both sides benefited while the capital cycle ran. When rates rose, founders discovered that revenue from an investor's network is a dependency, not a moat.

The oil industry wrote the same pattern earlier. American majors entered joint ventures with Gulf state producers, financed the infrastructure, supplied the technology, and held equity. The dependency appeared bilateral. Then the host governments nationalized the fields.

Anthropic holds the model weights. Google holds the compute. Amazon holds the second layer.

The independence is the pitch deck. The structure is something older.

content_pack.substack_draft:
The $200 billion number is doing all the work in this story.

Anthropic committed this week to spending $200 billion on Google Cloud over five years. Google has already invested up to $40 billion in Anthropic, with additional tranches tied to performance milestones. Anthropic also committed over $100 billion to AWS over a decade, where Amazon holds a separate $25 billion stake. The narrative around Anthropic has always been that it is the safety-focused independent lab, accountable to no one's ecosystem. That framing gets harder to maintain when you add up what independence costs.

I have been thinking about the Softbank era, 2017 to 2022, and how strategic investor relationships tend to reveal their true structure only under stress. Softbank funded, Softbank connected, Softbank extracted. The companies that raised from them got capital and captive customers. They also got a ceiling.

What I am not sure about is whether this structure is actually bad for Anthropic's mission, as opposed to its valuation. If Google's infrastructure is what it takes to run frontier AI at scale, then committing to it may be table stakes, not a concession. The question is whether the pricing terms, the renegotiation rights, and the equity performance triggers give Anthropic room to maneuver if Google's interests diverge from its own.

ideas.title: Software Never Traded Cheap. Until Now.
ideas.trend: Public SaaS companies now trade at a forward P/E discount to the S&P 500 for the first time in history, per SaaStr, after losing $2 trillion in market cap since late 2025.
ideas.consensus: SaaS valuations got overextended in 2020-2022 and are correcting back to sustainable levels as rates normalize.
ideas.angle: This is not a valuation correction. The market is pricing the structural end of seat-based licensing. AI agents do not buy seats. When agents replace headcount rather than complement it, the revenue model reverses.

content_pack.x_longform:
Most people frame the SaaS rout as a valuation correction. It is a pricing model verdict.

For the first time in history, public software companies trade at a forward P/E discount to the S&P 500, per SaaStr's analysis this month. Software multiples averaged 84.1x from 2020 to 2022. They now sit at 22.7x, below the broader market. IGV, the iShares Expanded Tech-Software ETF, is down more than 22 percent from its highs. Two trillion dollars in software market cap gone. Per SaaStr, that relative decline exceeds the dot-com bust, the financial crisis, and the 2022 rate shock combined.

The selloff accelerated in late January when Anthropic announced Claude Cowork, positioning a single agent layer as a replacement for the multi-application SaaS stack.

The usual defense is duration sensitivity. Higher rates compress long-dated cash flows. That story fit 2022. Rates are lower now, and the discount keeps widening.

The mechanism is seat math. Traditional SaaS sells access by headcount. Salesforce charges per seat. Workday charges per seat. ServiceNow charges per seat. The model assumes companies grow their workforce over time, adding seats as headcount rises. Seat growth equals ARR growth.

AI agents charge per token and per API call. The unit is tasks completed, not employees served. A company moving from 100 analysts to 10 analysts and 5 AI agents does not increase its SaaS spend. It compresses it.

Per SaaStr, roughly 75 percent of new hyperscaler infrastructure spending in 2026, more than $450 billion, targets AI infrastructure. Capital that used to flow into SaaS expansion budgets is redirecting toward the tools replacing those budgets.

The enterprise CIO now holds two competing line items: maintain the SaaS stack, or fund the AI stack that makes it optional. The market is pricing which one wins.

content_pack.substack_draft:
The SaaS premium is roughly thirteen years old now, and it was built on one assumption: recurring revenue tied to headcount is the most durable business model in software. Markets agreed, persistently. Ten times ARR was cheap. Twenty times ARR was fair. The premium was structural, not sentimental.

Per SaaStr's analysis this month, that assumption has cracked. Public software companies now trade at a forward P/E discount to the S&P 500 for the first time in the modern era. Software multiples averaged 84.1x at peak and now sit at 22.7x, below the broader market. The relative decline, per SaaStr, exceeds the dot-com bust in severity.

The interesting part is not the size of the drop. It is the timing. Rates are lower than they were in 2022, when software multiples last compressed sharply. The selloff accelerated in late January when Anthropic announced Claude Cowork, which positions an AI agent layer as a replacement for the multi-application SaaS stack rather than a complement to it.

I think the market is trying to answer a question no spreadsheet can cleanly model: at what scale do AI agents stop complementing human headcount and start replacing it? When that inflection point arrives, seat-based SaaS stops growing at the unit where it used to grow. The valuation premium disappears not because the product gets worse, but because the model does. I am genuinely unsure whether that inflection point is two years away or already here.

ideas.title: Export Controls Didn't Delay China. They Funded the Other Lane.
ideas.trend: China's Zhipu AI trained GLM-5, a 744B-parameter frontier model, on 100,000 Huawei Ascend chips with zero NVIDIA dependency, actively competing with GPT-5 and Claude after being placed on the US Entity List.
ideas.consensus: US export controls on AI chips are successfully slowing China's frontier AI development by cutting off access to NVIDIA's advanced GPUs.
ideas.angle: Export controls didn't slow China's AI. They forced China to build a full domestic compute stack from chip design to training framework to frontier model. The policy intended to create dependence created independence.

content_pack.x_longform:
The US banned NVIDIA chip sales to China. China responded by training a frontier model without a single American chip.

Zhipu AI was placed on the US Entity List in January 2025. No legal access to H100s, H200s, or B200s. So it trained GLM-5, a 744-billion parameter model, on 100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B processors using Huawei's own MindSpore framework. Released in February. Open-sourced under MIT. Frontier-class performance.

The policy intended to delay China's frontier AI by three to five years. It forced China to build a full domestic compute stack instead.

Export controls accelerated the race. In the other lane.
content_pack.x_thread:
Tweet 1: The country you sanction doesn't stop. It builds. China just proved it.

Tweet 2: Zhipu AI was placed on the US Entity List in January 2025. No legal access to NVIDIA H100s, H200s, or B200s. So it built its own path.

Tweet 3: GLM-5: 744B parameters. Trained on 100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B chips. Built on Huawei's MindSpore framework. 28.5 trillion tokens. Zero NVIDIA silicon.

Tweet 4: Performance: frontier-class. Rivals GPT-5 and Claude on major benchmarks per Artificial Analysis. Open-sourced under MIT license in February 2026.

Tweet 5: US export controls went into effect in October 2022. The stated goal: delay China's frontier AI development by 3-5 years.

Tweet 6: What happened instead: China now has a full domestic AI stack. HiSilicon designs the chips. SMIC fabs them at 7nm. MindSpore runs the training. GLM-5 proves the stack works.

Tweet 7: The export control policy assumed China would stall without NVIDIA. China assumed it would build. One assumption was correct.

Tweet 8: Export controls accelerated the race. In the other lane.
content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people think of the US AI chip export controls as a constraint on China. The more I read about GLM-5, the more I think they functioned as a forcing function.

Zhipu AI was placed on the US Entity List in January 2025, cutting off legal access to NVIDIA's advanced GPUs. In February 2026, Zhipu released GLM-5: a 744-billion parameter model trained on 100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B chips, using Huawei's own MindSpore framework across a 28.5-trillion-token training run. Frontier-class performance. Open-sourced under MIT. Not one American chip in the stack.

The policy was designed to delay China's frontier AI by three to five years. Whether the delay actually occurred is debatable. What is harder to debate is the secondary effect: China now has a domestic full-stack AI ecosystem, from chip design at HiSilicon to fabrication at SMIC to training framework to frontier model. That stack did not exist in 2022.

What I am not sure about is whether this was a predictable consequence that policymakers accepted as a price worth paying, or whether GLM-5 represents a genuine strategic surprise. The difference matters for what the next round of export controls looks like.
